back: Any substance taken into the body that modifies or affects chemical reactions in the body.
A drug used to prevent, treat or cure a disease, or to relieve its symptoms.
A medicinal drug that kills bacteria or stops them growing.
notes: Example: penicillin, from the mould Penicillium.

back: Alexander Fleming, in 1928, when bacteria did not grow near a Penicillium mould.
notes: It became a medicine in the 1940s.

front: Why don't antibiotics work against viruses?
back: Viruses are not cells: they lack the structures antibiotics attack and reproduce inside host cells.
notes: So antibiotics do not help colds, flu or HIV.

back: A few bacteria are resistant by mutation; the antibiotic kills the others; the resistant ones survive, reproduce and spread.
Methicillin-resistant *Staphylococcus aureus*: bacteria resistant to many antibiotics, causing hard-to-treat infections.

front: How can antibiotic resistance be limited?
back: Use antibiotics only when essential, take them exactly as prescribed, never share them, and avoid routine use in farm animals.
A painkiller, such as paracetamol or aspirin; it relieves pain but does not treat the cause.
A drug that kills Plasmodium in the blood or prevents infection, such as ACT.
Follow a health worker's directions, never share prescription medicines, check expiry dates, store safely and avoid unlicensed sellers.
